destination.title: Police Destroyed His Home Chasing a Stranger — Then Paid Him Nothing

short42: The nine-year-old got out safe. Behind him
an armed stranger fleeing police had broken
into the house at random
a family he'd never met.
For nineteen hours the home held.
Then it was gone.
So who pays for that?
Talks failed.
Police answered with gas and a BearCat
an armored truck that punched holes through the walls.
The order on record:
take as much of the building as
needed without making the roof fall in.
The family had done nothing wrong.
The city offered five thousand dollars for temporary lodging.
Their insurance excluded government acts. To rebuild
he borrowed a quarter of a million dollars.
So he sued.
But the courts called it police power
not a taking nothing owed. Their words:
the innocence of the property owner does
not factor into the determination. In 2020
the Supreme Court declined to hear it
deciding nothing at all.
Full story on the channel.
Follow for the cases they don't teach you.

candidate_payload_lines: Nobody who lived in that house had done anything at all.
Nobody gets to choose which door the emergency comes through.
Nobody in this story did the wrong thing that day.
What Leo Lech would spend the next years arguing about was never whether the police should have destroyed the house.
Somewhere in that pile was a nine-year-old's room, and the boy who had walked out of it at the start of all this never came back to it.
Five years of a man's life, moved, because a stranger he'd never met chose that door.
And no one in this had done anything wrong.
In January 2018, a federal district court in Colorado ruled against him, and its reasoning had two moves.
On October 29, 2019, the Tenth Circuit affirmed, a panel of Judges Holmes, McKay and Moritz, with Judge Nancy Moritz writing.
It reached back to an 1887 case, Mugler v.
In October 2025 the Seventh Circuit rejected her claim.
Her insurer covered none of the police damage.
In 2024 the Sixth Circuit called a categorical police-power exception questionable, then dismissed the claim anyway on an old common-law privilege attached to searches and arrests.
In November 2025 the Ninth Circuit ruled that Carlos Pena gets nothing.
Thirteen hours earlier, in August 2022, an armed fugitive had shoved Pena out of his own print shop in Los Angeles and locked the door behind him.
Nobody disputes the police acted lawfully.
In November 2024, when the Supreme Court declined to hear Vicki Baker's case, Justice Sotomayor wrote a statement respecting that denial, joined by Justice Gorsuch.
In May 2026, eleven years after his son's house was opened with explosives and six years after the Supreme Court declined to hear him, Leo Lech signed his name to a brief in someone else's case.

lines.text: Every side of this argument quotes the same sentence, from a 1960 case.
source_lines: Justice Sotomayor and the parties on every side of this quote the same sentence, from a 1960 case called Armstrong.

lines.text: The Takings Clause was designed to bar Government from forcing some people alone to bear public burdens which, in all fairness and justice, should be borne by the public as a whole.
source_lines: The Takings Clause was designed to bar Government from forcing some people alone to bear public burdens which, in all fairness and justice, should be borne by the public as a whole.

lines.text: Some people alone. In November 2024, when the Supreme Court declined one of these cases, Justice Sotomayor wrote a statement respecting that denial, joined by Justice Gorsuch.
source_lines: Some people alone.
In November 2024, when the Supreme Court declined to hear Vicki Baker's case, Justice Sotomayor wrote a statement respecting that denial, joined by Justice Gorsuch. It carried no legal weight.

lines.text: She wrote that the question divides the courts of appeals, and that it would benefit from further percolation in the lower courts before the Court steps in. The denial expressed no view on the merits.
source_lines: She wrote that the case raises an important question that divides the courts of appeals, whether the Takings Clause requires compensation when the government damages private property under its police power.
And she said the question would benefit from further percolation in the lower courts before the Court steps in, adding that the denial expressed no view on the merits.

lines.text: The statement carried no legal weight. It was not the Court's opinion, and not a dissent.
source_lines: It carried no legal weight. It wasn't the Court's opinion and it wasn't a dissent. It was filed alongside the refusal itself.

lines.text: She mapped the split, several circuits one way, and the Fourth holding police-power action is not automatically exempt.
source_lines: She mapped the split: the Seventh Circuit and the Federal Circuit on one side, the Sixth reaching the same result by another road, the Fourth Circuit holding that government action under the police power is not automatically exempt from the Takings Clause.
